metadata.title: Grok Bot, Built: Futurama-Toy Enterprise
metadata.topic: BLENDER BUILD · HOW TO BUILD IT
metadata.render_by: Professor Bear, with his own tools (beat sheet only)
metadata.display_rule: Viewers only ever see or hear 'the Liam voice'. No subtitles, no captions, no .srt. Hand-build steps are labelled as a Blender UI reconstruction.

beats.narration_text: This is Liam. This is the starship Enterprise, reimagined as a chunky Futurama-style vinyl toy. Grok Bot built it in Blender, entirely from Python, run headless, in nine rounds. First, walk around it. Then: if you wanted to build this yourself, by hand, in Blender, how would you do it?
beats.new_visual_element: Round 9 · hero three-quarter

shot.label: Round 9 · hero three-quarter

beats.narration_text: An inflated saucer with a red rubber bumper. A bubble-dome bridge. A pudgy egg of a secondary hull, and two fat sausage nacelles with red caps. It's a generic toy design. No registry number, no logos, no insignia.
beats.new_visual_element: Front three-quarter · side · rear three-quarter

shot.label: Front three-quarter · side · rear three-quarter

beats.narration_text: From the front, the saucer is a wide lens over the hull and nacelles. From above, the saucer covers most of the secondary hull. From below, the sensor hub and the stepped cream deflector.
beats.new_visual_element: Front · top · below

shot.label: Front · top · below

beats.narration_text: Up close. The bridge: a cream ring, a clear dome and a knob inside. The nacelle, with cream rings and rivets. And the deflector: a stepped cream housing with a dark dish, spokes and a cone.
beats.new_visual_element: Details: bridge · nacelle · deflector · contact sheet

shot.label: Details: bridge · nacelle · deflector · contact sheet

beats.narration_text: The brief had two inputs. Professor Bear's blueprint images of the Enterprise, for the layout. And a concept image Grok Bot generated, for the style. It's an AI image, not a photo. Professor Bear said: I love it. It's fun. You definitely recognize the enterprise, but it's not the enterprise. That made the concept the style target.
beats.new_visual_element: Style target: the Grok Bot concept image (AI image)

shot.label: Style target: the Grok Bot concept image (AI image)

ai_did.summary: Concept image as style target; blueprint ratios as the starting layout (BUILD_NOTES Sources and Measurements).

ui_steps.label: Blender UI reconstruction (hypothetical, not a recorded session)
steps: Add the blueprint views as Reference images (Add → Image → Reference) in the front, side and top orthographic views.
Put the concept image on a camera as a Background Image for the hero view.
Lock the reference objects so they can't be selected while you model.

beats.narration_text: Block it out with shapes that turn. The script's saucer is a lathe around the vertical axis: a superellipse profile, a hundred and twenty-one points, spun into a hundred and twenty-eight segments. Radius one, top height point three two, bottom point two four. The secondary hull is another lathe, around the length, from an eight-point profile. The nacelles are lathes too, with red caps.
beats.new_visual_element: AI did: saucer, hull and nacelles are lathes

shot.label: AI did: saucer, hull and nacelles are lathes

ai_did.summary: lathe(): saucer from a 121-point superellipse profile (R 1.0, Ht 0.32, Hb 0.24, exponents 1.9 / 2.1), 128 segments; secondary hull from hull_prof (8 points) around X; nacelles lathed around X.

beats.narration_text: By hand, you'd draw half of each profile as a line of vertices against the blueprint, then spin it with a screw modifier. One profile for the saucer, one for the hull, one for a nacelle. Shade smooth. The whole ship is three drawings and three modifiers before any detail.
beats.new_visual_element: By hand: draw half the profile → Screw modifier

shot.label: By hand: draw half the profile → Screw modifier

ui_steps.label: Blender UI reconstruction (hypothetical, not a recorded session)
steps: Front orthographic view (Numpad 1); Add → Mesh → Plane, merge to one vertex (M → At Center).
Tab into Edit Mode; Ctrl+right-click to place vertices along half the saucer's outline over the blueprint.
Modifier tab → Add Modifier → Generate → Screw; Axis Z, Steps 64 to 128, Merge on.
Repeat for the secondary hull and one nacelle with Axis X.
Object → Shade Smooth (or Shade Auto Smooth).

beats.narration_text: Proportions came from the blueprint first. Saucer diameter one. Nacelles about one point two six saucer diameters long, at plus or minus point three eight off the centreline. Then in round five, Grok Bot re-measured everything off the concept, and the whole ship became much more compact, with the hull pulled forward under the saucer. Grok Bot calls it the biggest single improvement.
beats.new_visual_element: Blueprint ratios → re-measured off the concept (round 5)

shot.label: Blueprint ratios → re-measured off the concept (round 5)

ai_did.summary: Blueprint ratios (saucer 1.0, nacelles ~1.26 long at ±0.38); round 5 re-measured off the concept: nacelle front x ≈ -1.0, spacing ±0.7, hull front x ≈ -0.5.

ui_steps.label: Blender UI reconstruction (hypothetical, not a recorded session)
steps: Scale the saucer to exactly 2 units across (N panel → Dimensions) and measure everything as a ratio of it.
Place the nacelles and hull from those ratios with G and typed values (G X -1.0).
Switch to the hero camera and adjust against the concept; write the new numbers down.

beats.narration_text: The order the script builds in is a good order for a person. The saucer, then the red bumper and its lights, the porthole rings, and the bridge. The sensor hub underneath. Then the secondary hull, its deflector, the end cap and the red side stripes. Then the neck and the pylons, lofted beams with cream piping. Then the nacelles. Last, the studio.
beats.new_visual_element: Build order: saucer → hull → neck and pylons → nacelles → studio

shot.label: Build order: saucer → hull → neck and pylons → nacelles → studio

ai_did.summary: build.py sections: SAUCER (bumper, lights, portholes, bridge, sensor hub) → SECONDARY HULL (deflector, end cap, stripe panels) → beams (neck, pylons) → NACELLES → staging.

ui_steps.label: Blender UI reconstruction (hypothetical, not a recorded session)
steps: Big shapes first, then the parts that join them (neck, pylons), then small details.
Neck and pylons: Add → Mesh → Cube, scale into a beam, bevel the edges, rotate to connect hull and nacelle.
Parent each detail to its main shape (Ctrl+P) so moving the hull moves its parts.

beats.narration_text: Modifiers. This build uses almost none. The only one in the script is bevel, on the little bumper lights and the hull lights. There's a subdivision option in the code, but it's never switched on. The smoothness comes from dense lathes instead. No mirror modifier: each nacelle and pylon is built in a loop, one side, then the other. No booleans either. That bevelled little cube is also why the bumper lights look like stuck-on tiles.
beats.new_visual_element: AI did: bevel only · no subdivision · no mirror · no boolean

shot.label: AI did: bevel only · no subdivision · no mirror · no boolean

ai_did.summary: Only BEVEL modifiers (bumper lights: width 0.012, 3 segments; hull lights: width 0.014). new_obj/lathe have a sub parameter but every call leaves it 0. Nacelles built in `for side,tag in ((1,'P'),(-1,'S'))`.

beats.narration_text: By hand, you'd use more. A mirror modifier on the nacelles and pylons, so one side drives both. A screw for the turned shapes. A subdivision surface for the soft vinyl look. And for the bumper lights, shape them into the bumper with a boolean or a shrinkwrap, so they read as part of the toy, not tiles stuck on top.
beats.new_visual_element: By hand: mirror · screw · subdivision · shrinkwrap the lights

shot.label: By hand: mirror · screw · subdivision · shrinkwrap the lights

ui_steps.label: Blender UI reconstruction (hypothetical, not a recorded session)
steps: Nacelle and pylon: Add Modifier → Mirror, axis Y, mirror object the saucer (centred at the origin).
Subdivision Surface (Ctrl+2) on the saucer, hull and nacelles; add support loops (Ctrl+R) at the rims.
Bumper lights: Shrinkwrap modifier targeting the bumper, or Boolean Union then remesh.
Bevel last on hard-edged parts.

beats.narration_text: Six materials: a glossy grey-blue vinyl, cream, red, a dark slate, white, and clear glass. And one colour lesson. In round one, the colours came out pastel and washed out, under Blender's default view transform. Round two switched to standard, and the slate colours came back. By hand, it's one setting, in colour management.
beats.new_visual_element: Six materials · view transform: Standard

shot.label: Six materials · view transform: Standard

ai_did.summary: mat() per params colour: body #8797A6, cream #DCC594, red #CF4F37, dark #45545F, white #E9E7E0; view_transform 'Standard' from round 2 (round 1 was the default AgX).

ui_steps.label: Blender UI reconstruction (hypothetical, not a recorded session)
steps: Material tab → New → Principled BSDF; Base Color hex 8797A6; Roughness about 0.24.
Render properties → Color Management → View Transform: Standard, Look: None.
Glass: Transmission Weight 1.0, low roughness, for the bridge dome.

beats.narration_text: Lighting: five area lights, a key, a fill, a top, a rim and a front, in Cycles with the denoiser on, sixty-four samples. The ground is a shadow catcher, so the ship renders on a transparent background, and a small script lays it over a soft grey gradient. The hero camera sits low, about sixty degrees off the nose, with a forty-five millimetre lens. The side, top and front views are orthographic, to sit over the blueprints.
beats.new_visual_element: Five area lights · shadow catcher · 45 mm hero · orthographic blueprint views

shot.label: Five area lights · shadow catcher · 45 mm hero · orthographic blueprint views

ai_did.summary: Area lights Key/Fill/Top/Rim/Front; Cycles CPU, OIDN, 64 samples; film_transparent + is_shadow_catcher ground; comp.py gradient; hero (az 60, el 6, d 5.5, 45 mm); side/top/front ORTHO in render.py.

ui_steps.label: Blender UI reconstruction (hypothetical, not a recorded session)
steps: Add a plane under the ship; Object properties → Visibility → Shadow Catcher.
Render properties → Film → Transparent.
Camera properties → Type: Orthographic for the blueprint views; set Orthographic Scale to frame them.
Hero camera: Focal Length 45 mm, low and about 60° off the nose.

beats.narration_text: Checking. Only one view can be checked directly against the concept, because the concept is a single image. So the hero camera was fitted to it. The blueprint views check layout only. In round nine, the top view caught the pylons reading as wide plates, so they were narrowed.
beats.new_visual_element: Hero vs concept · top vs blueprint

shot.label: Hero vs concept · top vs blueprint

ai_did.summary: compare.py builds render-vs-reference sheets: hero vs concept, side/top/front vs blueprint; round 9 narrowed the pylons after the top view.

beats.narration_text: Export. A separate script opens the saved file, applies the modifiers and writes the G L B, without saving over the dot blend. By hand: File, Export, glTF two point oh, G L B, apply modifiers. The G L B carries flat colours only. The glass, lights and render setup stay in Blender.
beats.new_visual_element: File → Export → glTF 2.0 (.glb)

shot.label: File → Export → glTF 2.0 (.glb)

ai_did.summary: export.py: export_scene.gltf(export_format='GLB', export_apply=True); writes stats; does not save the .blend.

ui_steps.label: Blender UI reconstruction (hypothetical, not a recorded session)
steps: File → Export → glTF 2.0 (.glb/.gltf); Format glTF Binary.
Data → Mesh → Apply Modifiers on.
Re-import the .glb into a new scene and check the colours.

beats.narration_text: The rounds, in one strip. Round one, pastel. Round two, real colours and fatter nacelles. Round three, the deflector. Round five, the big re-measure. Round seven, a double red bumper and an eye-level camera. Round eight, a flatter, lens-like saucer top. Round nine, narrower pylons.
beats.new_visual_element: Rounds 1 to 9, hero camera

shot.label: Rounds 1 to 9, hero camera

beats.narration_text: Grok Bot's own score: about six out of ten. Hero six; side, top and front five each, for layout only; the details six. It's clearly the same toy design. But next to the concept it's thinner. The saucer is too thin. The secondary hull is too small. The neck is barely visible. And the bumper lights look like tiles.
beats.new_visual_element: Round 9: Grok Bot about 6/10

shot.label: Round 9: Grok Bot about 6/10

beats.narration_text: Professor Bear judged the concept, not this model. His verdict on round nine is still pending. Right after the concept, he sent an STL kit, but that kit is the Planet Express ship, and it went into that ship's round fifteen. This one hasn't had a human verdict yet. Until it does, the six is only Grok Bot's opinion.
beats.new_visual_element: Professor Bear: round 9 verdict pending

shot.label: Professor Bear: round 9 verdict pending

beats.narration_text: What the evidence doesn't establish. The concept was measured assuming a camera about sixty-two degrees off the nose. That angle is an assumption, so the measured sizes are only as good as that guess. The blueprints are a different, non-toy style, so they can't score the look. And the hand steps here are a reconstruction. Nobody has built this toy by hand to test them.
beats.new_visual_element: Not established

shot.label: Not established

beats.narration_text: So, to build it yourself. Three turned shapes first. Proportions as ratios of the saucer. Details in order, big to small. Modifiers to do the repetition for you. Check the hero view against the concept, every round. And keep a person in the loop, because only a person can say whether it's fun.
beats.new_visual_element: Turn · measure · order · modifiers · compare · a human in the loop

shot.label: Turn · measure · order · modifiers · compare · a human in the loop

beats.narration_text: Grok Bot, Built. This is Liam.
